## Goals

- Know what GlassNN is for, and what it deliberately leaves out.
- Install GlassNN and run a first computation.
- Understand the array backend and why every operation goes through `backend.xp`.
- Choose between float32 and float64, and know why gradient checks need float64.

## Theory

### What a neural-network library does

A neural-network library does three jobs:

1. it stores numbers in multidimensional arrays (*tensors*) and computes with them;
2. it computes derivatives of those computations automatically (@sec-autodiff);
3. it provides building blocks: layers, losses and optimizers (later chapters).

Production libraries such as PyTorch do these jobs in compiled code, tuned for
speed. GlassNN does them in a few thousand lines of plain Python on top of
NumPy [@harris2020array], so that each step can be read, printed and changed.
It uses PyTorch's names (`Tensor`, `backward`, `no_grad`, later `Module`,
`Linear`, `zero_grad`, `step`), so code written with GlassNN transfers almost
line by line.

GlassNN is not fast at scale, does not load pretrained models, and has no
in-place operations. These are deliberate choices: every one of them would
make the code longer and harder to read.

### Arrays and the backend

A `Tensor` holds an array of numbers in its attribute `.data`. All arithmetic
is *vectorized*: one call such as `a.data * b.data` processes every element in
compiled NumPy code, which is orders of magnitude faster than a Python loop
over the elements.

GlassNN never calls NumPy directly. It calls `backend.xp`, the *active array
module*. Today that is always NumPy. Because CuPy implements the same API on
NVIDIA GPUs, switching `backend.xp` to CuPy runs the same code on a GPU; this
optional backend is the subject of a later chapter.

### Floating-point numbers

A floating-point number stores a sign, an exponent and a significand of $p$
bits. The spacing between 1 and the next representable number is the
*machine epsilon* $\varepsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{1-p}$, and every arithmetic
operation is exact up to a relative error of at most half of it:

$$
\operatorname{fl}(x \circ y) = (x \circ y)(1 + \delta),
\qquad |\delta| \le u = \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{\text{mach}},
$$ {#eq-rounding}

where $\circ$ is one of $+, -, \times, /$ and $u$ is the *unit roundoff*
[@goodfellow2016deep, chap. 4].

| dtype | significand bits $p$ | $\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}$ | bytes per number |
|---|---|---|---|
| float32 | 24 | $2^{-23} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7}$ | 4 |
| float64 | 53 | $2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ | 8 |

Training a network tolerates float32 well: stochastic gradients are noisy
anyway, and float32 halves the memory and doubles the arithmetic throughput.
GlassNN therefore uses **float32 by default**, like PyTorch. Checking
gradients numerically (@sec-autodiff) compares two quantities that agree only
to a fraction of the available digits, so the tests and gradient checks use
**float64**.

### The dtype rule

When a tensor is created, its dtype follows one rule:

- an explicit `dtype=` always wins;
- otherwise floating-point input (Python floats, lists of floats, NumPy arrays
  of *any* float dtype) becomes the default dtype;
- integer and boolean input keeps its dtype (integers are used as indices and
  class labels).

::: {.callout-warning title="Differences from PyTorch"}
`torch.tensor(np.ones(3))` keeps the float64 dtype of the NumPy array.
GlassNN casts it to the default dtype, so that data created with NumPy (which
defaults to float64) never silently mixes with float32 parameters.
:::

## Try it

### Installation

GlassNN needs Python 3.13 or newer. Install a tagged release with `pip` or
`uv` directly from GitHub (no PyPI package is published):

```bash
pip install "glassnn @ git+https://github.com/bioinfo-recetox/glassnn@v0.1.0"
```

To work on the library itself, clone the repository and run
`uv sync --extra dev`, then `uv run pytest`.

### A first computation

```{python}
import numpy as np

import glassnn
from glassnn import Tensor, backend

print(glassnn.__version__, backend.get_backend(), backend.get_default_dtype())
x = Tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
x, x.shape, x.dtype
```

The dtype rule in action: a float64 NumPy array becomes float32, integers stay
integers.

```{python}
Tensor(np.ones(3)).dtype, Tensor(np.arange(3)).dtype, Tensor([1, 2], dtype="float64").dtype
```

### Rounding

In float32, adding $10^{-8}$ to 1 changes nothing, because $10^{-8}$ is below
the unit roundoff $u \approx 6 \times 10^{-8}$ (@eq-rounding). In float64 the
sum is exact enough to differ from 1.

```{python}
print(np.finfo(np.float32).eps, np.finfo(np.float64).eps)
print("float32:", (Tensor([1.0]) + 1e-8).item() == 1.0)

backend.set_default_dtype("float64")
print("float64:", (Tensor([1.0]) + 1e-8).item() == 1.0)
backend.set_default_dtype("float32")
```

## Exercises

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.1: memory"}
How many bytes does a $1000 \times 1000$ tensor take in float32 and in
float64? Check your answer with `.data.nbytes`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
$10^6$ numbers of 4 and 8 bytes: 4 MB and 8 MB.

```{python}
Tensor(np.zeros((1000, 1000))).data.nbytes, Tensor(np.zeros((1000, 1000)), dtype="float64").data.nbytes
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.2: summation order"}
Add $10^6$ copies of $0.1$ in float32, once one after the other
(`np.cumsum(...)[-1]`) and once with `np.sum`. Which is closer to $10^5$, and
why?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{python}
values = np.full(10**6, 0.1, dtype=np.float32)
print("one after the other:", np.cumsum(values)[-1])
print("np.sum:             ", np.sum(values))
```

Sequential summation makes an error of up to $u$ relative to the running sum
at each step, and the running sum grows to $10^5$, so the errors add up to a
visible amount. `np.sum` uses *pairwise* summation, which adds numbers of
similar size, so its error grows only logarithmically with the number of
terms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.3: the dtype rule"}
Predict the dtype of `Tensor(np.ones(3, dtype=np.float16))`,
`Tensor([True, False])` and `Tensor(3)`, then check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
float32 (any floating input becomes the default dtype), bool and int64
(non-floating input keeps its dtype).

```{python}
Tensor(np.ones(3, dtype=np.float16)).dtype, Tensor([True, False]).dtype, Tensor(3).dtype
```
:::
